events.name: Nyob Zoo Xyoo Tshiab! Blessings from the Hmong New Year Table
events.description: Rhythms, Roots, Recipes: Community Stories of Food and Music brings together cooking demonstrations, live music, and storytelling. Each program in the series explores traditions that animate families and communities across the United States—and beyond. Hmong New Year is a time to celebrate the end of the harvest season while washing away any bitterness and hardship faced during the previous year. Across the Hmong diaspora, it also is an opportunity to renew ancestral ties and impart cultural lessons to the next generation. Join us as Minneapolis-based, award-winning chef Diane Moua prepares traditional Hmong dishes including nqaj npua tsawg (Hmong pulled pork), pickled mustard greens, sticky rice, and tuav kuas txoj (hot sauce). While Moua cooks, Tiffany Xyooj will perform Hmong folksongs that reference staple ingredients and migration, each echoing the voices and hopes of those who came before. This lively conversation will be facilitated by KaYing Yang of the social enterprise RedGreen Rivers. Noj Tsab/Tsiab Peb Caug!

events.name: Pakeezah
events.description: New 4K Restoration! Following our Diwali celebration, enjoy this beloved Bollywood classic, a heartbreaking romance with gorgeous visuals and some of the most beautiful songs ever committed to film. Set against the backdrop of the courtly era of the Nawabs of Lucknow, Pakeezah is a poetically exquisite classic that took fourteen years to complete. The film’s painterly frames are saturated with color, opulent sets and costumes, haunting music, and actress Meena Kumari in an unforgettable performance. The courtesan Nargis is rejected by the family of her husband Shahabuddin and dies giving birth to her daughter Sahibjaan who grows up to become a renowned courtesan. But she lives in a gilded cage, yearning for love and a life of dignity. Her life takes a turn when a forest officer, Salim, accidentally encounters her while she is asleep in a train compartment. Captivated by her, he leaves behind a note praising her beauty and innocence without knowing her identity. Their paths cross again and they fall in love. However, misunderstandings and the stigma attached to Sahibjaan’s identity threaten to keep them apart. Description adapted from Film Heritage Foundation. Pakeezah was restored in 4K by Film Heritage Foundation at L’Immagine Ritrovata laboratory in association with Bilal Amrohi of Lionheart Cinema. Director: Kamal Amrohi. Country: India. Released: 1972. Length: 153 min. Format: DCP. Language: Urdu with English subtitles. Image courtesy of the Film Heritage Foundation

events.description: Seating is limited. Reserve your seat in advance to pick where you sit ($6 fee per order). Join the standby line for remaining seats on the day of the concert, free of charge. Pianist Eunbi Kim’s sonic memoir it feels like a dream features a soundworld of classical music threaded with an indie-pop awareness. Meanwhile, hypnotic projected visuals by new media artist Xuan expand the experience. This immersive multimedia performance explores questions of family and identity, offering listeners a space to meditate on the dreams they carry and pass on. it feels like a dream includes works by Daniel Bernard Roumain (DBR), Angélica Negrón, Pauchi Sasaki, and Sophia Jani for piano, pre-recorded voices, and electronics, written for and performed by Kim. The evening also premieres The Dreamers , a new work by Corey Chang written for Kim and commissioned by the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art. The work incorporates a poem that Kim’s father wrote more than thirty years ago, shortly after immigrating to the US from Korea—a meditation on the duality of hope and despondency experienced by immigrants navigating a new land. This performance is part of the Bill and Mary Meyer Concert Series. The Bill and Mary Meyer Concert Series is generously made possible by the Bill and Mary Meyer Concert Series Endowment. events.description: Fall in love with an evening of cinema and conversation. This Cinema + Conversation features a French-inspired dinner, a screening of Montmartre, and a conversation with the film’s writer and director, Leon Hendrix III, producer Maurice D. Hendrix, and stars Ito Aghayere and Jesse Williams. The evening begins at 5:30 pm with a French-inspired dinner, inviting guests to experience the flavors and atmosphere of France before journeying to Paris through the film. After dinner, guests will head to the Oprah Winfrey Theater for the 7:00 pm screening of Montmartre. Montmartre tells the story of a woman dissatisfied with her increasingly disconnected life; Jo travels to the storied Parisian neighborhood of Montmartre, where she meets Toussaint, a tour guide who loves poetry, magic, and romance. As the two grow closer, culture, art, and love intertwine, reconnecting Jo with a passion for life she thought she had lost. A moderated conversation will follow the screening with Leon, Maurice, Ito, and Jesse about the making of Montmartre and the film’s exploration of art, culture, place, romance, and rediscovery. events.name: History in the Making: Carter G. Woodson Zine Lab
events.description: What happens when art meets history at the museum? Join artist Brittany Mona' to make zines—small booklets that offer a creative way to tell a story or explore an idea. This hands-on, family-friendly workshop is inspired by the life and legacy of Carter G. Woodson, historian, educator, and longtime resident of DC’s Shaw neighborhood. Known as the “Father of Black History, Dr. Woodson worked with artists like Loïs Mailou Jones to publish illustrated books and journals about African American history for learners of all ages. At the time, Black history was seldom included in historical narratives. The program commemorates the 100th anniversary of Black History Month, founded by Dr. Woodson in 1926, and is offered in partnership with the Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site, National Park Service in honor of its grand reopening on November 7. Visitors can see books and journals by Dr. Woodson by visiting the museum’s current exhibition, We Make History, which explores stories of Washingtonians who work to improve our communities and those who record and share our history. History is in the making, and everyone can participate! Through history, art, and imagination, participants will leave with their own handmade zine and a deeper understanding of Carter G. Woodson’s legacy—and new ways of thinking about and making history!

events.name: First Light
events.description: Followed by a conversation with director James J. Robinson and a reception featuring Australian wine and snacks from the Philippines! This screening is copresented with the Embassy of the Philippines and the Embassy of Australia in celebration of the 80th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the Philippines and the United States and Australia. Watch the Trailer Australia’s official 99th Academy Awards entry is an elegant and quietly devastating examination of belief, community, and institutional corruption in a mountain community, centered around a rustic nuns’ convent and a conspicuously majestic church. Forty-something Sister Yolanda (Ruby Ruiz) lives in a colonial mountain convent and works at the local hospital where she is admired for her kindness and piety. After giving last rites to a young man involved in a horrific construction accident, the nun is troubled by the nature of his death. She starts to piece together the circumstances of the accident in her gentle way and through her interactions with those in her close-knit community, including the dead man’s father, the local priest, and the wealthy wife of the construction site owner. In discerning anew the power structures around her—including the center of her world, her beloved Church—her belief system and the very reason for her existence is put into question. Filipino-Australian director Robinson brings a distinguished background in photography to his first feature, with its long takes and painterly tableaux-style mise en scène. His restrained, patient approach lends dignity and observance to the characters, allowing them to be seen, in their wrongdoings and their kindness, through minute glances and soothing words. Description adapted from the International Film Festival Rotterdam. Director: James J. Robinson. Countries: Australia, Philippines. Released: 2025. Length: 118 min. Format: DCP. events.description: Join the History Film Forum for a screening of the Emmy-nominated Netflix documentary Join or Die ! Join or Die follows the half-century story of America’s civic unraveling through the journey of legendary social scientist Robert Putnam, whose groundbreaking “Bowling Alone” research into America’s decades-long decline in community connections could hold the answers to our democracy’s present crisis. Flanked by influential fans and scholars, as well as inspiring groups building community in neighborhoods across the country, join Bob as he explores three urgent civic questions: What makes democracy work? Why is American democracy in crisis? And, most importantly… What can we do about it? After the screening, join us for a conversation with the film's producers as we talk about the history of social groups, associations, and clubs- and why you should join one! _____________________ The National Museum of American History welcomes visitors of all ages and abilities. events.name: Teen Studio: Head Outside!
events.description: Teens: Ready to level up your art? Join us for Teen Studio, a free art-making program exclusively for teens ages 13–19. Push your artistic boundaries using materials and techniques inspired by artists whose work is now on view at the Hirshhorn. Dive into the Hirshhorn’s newly renovated Sculpture Garden with weekly workshops inspired by sculptures on view. This Saturday, take inspiration from Yoshitomo Nara’s Garden installation Sentinels of Stillness . Nara’s large sculptures are enlargements of hand-molded clay heads that originally fit in the palm of a hand. After learning about Nara, head back to Art School to work with guest artist Kaila Garcia to create your own clay head. Guest Artist Kaila Garcia is a Filipino American visual artist and art educator based in Washington, DC, whose work celebrates identity, culture, and community through sculptural portraiture. Her work challenges beauty standards while creating space for belonging, cultural pride, and self-definition. Her work has been exhibited at venues across Washington, DC, including the National Cherry Blossom Festival, Joan Hisaoka Healing Arts Gallery, and Femme Art Fair. In 2025, she received a DC Arts and Humanities Fellowship Grant in recognition of her artistic practice. Garcia earned her BFA from the University of the District of Columbia, graduating Magna Cum Laude, after studying at the Duke Ellington School of the Arts. Drop in to Teen Studio every Saturday between 2:30 and 4:30 PM. Register for the entire school year here (one-time registration covers all sessions). Join one session or join them all! Meet in Art School on the Museum’s Lower Level. Looking for more? Explore Art School Everywhere , wherever you are, to learn about artists in the Hirshhorn collection and get creative any time. ABOUT TEEN STUDIO Teens ages 13–19 are invited to hang out and get creative at the Hirshhorn’s Teen Studio . Teen Studio is a free series of art-making workshops offered from 2:30 to 4:30 PM every Saturday. All skill levels are welcome—from the novice notebook doodler to the experienced teen artist, there’s something for everyone! Each month, we’ll dive into a fresh theme inspired by artists on view. Each workshop will offer a mix of time in the galleries, where we’ll encounter groundbreaking artists, and time in Hirshhorn Art School, where we’ll experiment with new media and materials. events.description: Trading the Black Friday rush for Coffee & Gratitude at Smithsonian's Anacostia Community Museum, a gathering centered on art, storytelling, and gratitude. Start your morning with us and enjoy a light refreshments, coffee, and hot chocolate starting 10AM before settling in for a morning of creativity, reflection, and family fun.Visitors are invited to participate in Cyanotype Portraits: Gratitude Family Workshop, a hands-on art experience inspired by the people, memories, objects and moments for which we are thankful. Using photographs, natural materials, and light-sensitive paper, participants will create one-of-a-kind cyanotype portraits and keepsakes that celebrate family, connection, and the stories we carry. What is cyanotype? Cyanotype is a photographic printing process that uses light-sensitive materials and exposure to light to create distinctive blue-and-white images. Participants can arrange photographs, plants, and other objects on specially prepared paper and expose their designs to light, revealing a unique print.Guests can also join a guided tour of We Make History , ACM’s exhibition exploring how everyday people make, preserve, and share history. Discover the stories of changemakers and history keepers across the greater Washington, D.C. region and consider the people, places, and experiences that shape the histories we create together. Enjoy a cup of coffee or hot chocolate while creating, reflecting, and spending time together. Coffee & Gratitude offers an opportunity to slow down, share what you are grateful for, explore community stories, and create something meaningful to take home. events.description: Mark Native American Heritage Day with the museum with dance performances, a closer look at the installation Making a Statement , and hands-on activities. SCHEDULE OF EVENTS Level 1, Potomac Atrium 11:30 AM, 1:30 PM, 3:30 PM | Jingle Dress Dancing with Denmi Whiteman Learn about the significance of the Jingle Dress and enjoy dance performances by Denmi Whiteman (Oglala Lakota and Southern Cheyenne), who hails from the Pine Ridge reservation located in South Dakota. Whiteman is a published model, content creator, artist, old-style Jingle Dress dancer, and Native American advocate. Whiteman brings her culture and community into every space she enters. Level 3, imagiNATIONS Activity Center 10:30-11 AM | Story Time Families are invited to an interactive story time featuring the children’s book We Are Grateful by Traci Sorrell (Cherokee Nation). Attendees will have the opportunity to engage with objects from the museum's Teaching Collection such as photographs, textiles, or natural materials that can deepen their understanding of the community represented in the story, along with a craft or other activity. * Due to limited capacity in our spaces, tickets may be needed to enter the Activity Center and therefore the Story room (limited to 25 persons max). Please see staff at the entrance desk of the imagiNATIONS Activity Center on Level 3. **Recommended for visitors ages 3-9 years old accompanied by an adult caregiver. 11 AM–1PM and 2–4 PM | Hands On: Button-making Celebrate Native American Heritage Day by designing your own magnetic button. Level 4, Stretching the Canvas 11 AM–1PM and 2–4 PM | Inspired to Create Experience the gallery through the lens of color! Learn how artists use color to create mood, movement, and meaning, then put your observations into practice by designing a vibrant color-study bookmark. Experiment with palettes, patterns, and artistic techniques as you create a unique keepsake inspired by the artwork around you. Perfect for curious learners, budding artists, and visitors of all ages. Level 3, Making a Statement Special Installation 1 PM | Closer Look: Making a Statement Curator Anya Montiel (Mestiza/Tohono O'odham descent) offers a closer look at the museum’s special installation Making a Statement , which demonstrates how Native women combine traditional design elements with modern military symbolism to demonstrate cultural pride and honor military service. The installation features a historical Lakota beaded dress decorated with elaborate patriotic American imagery and a jingle dress made by members of the Native American Women Warriors to show pride in their Indigenous heritage and to emphasize the role of Native women in the military. Get hands-on to learn more about beadwork, jingle cones, and other design elements related to Native dressmaking in the museum’s Teaching Collection. Image: Photo courtesy of Denmi Whiteman
